editorialNote.title: Community-facing note, not a timeline event
body: Thank you very much for reading this timeline.
Dance, as an art form, suffers from its volatile nature.
Scholars all over the world are trying to mitigate flaws in recent decades.
To us, Shufflers, being both a rave and a social media culture creates unique challenges that most people do not care about.
This timeline is a collaborative work built to provide a historically accurate, informative, digestible and trustworthy source about Shuffling history, its years and constant changes.
It has required years of research and verification so new Shufflers and enthusiasts can learn without major doubts.
Remember: it is an endless work in progress.
If you have information to add or change, contact the project so it can be updated.

timeline.title: House and Techno
points: House and Techno emerged from the black and gay scenes in the USA.
elements: USA, Canada, Germany, Colombia and Ecuador flags appear near the underground-era baseline.

timeline.title: Aciiiiiied !!!
points: Foundations of the raves and Shuffling, as well as the first rave dance style known today as UK Rave Stepping.
Dropfoot was the local terminology; Foot Patrol are identified as pioneers.
The Second Summer of Love and Manchester are identified as cultural breakthroughs.
Acid House, Breakbeat and Jungle are listed as musical context.
Leeroy Thornhill, from The Prodigy, is named as a major influence on Melbourne ravers.
Running Man appears as a ghetto dance fad, with Janet Jackson, MC Hammer and Vanilla Ice named in the image.
elements: Large UK flag, smiley icon, acid/rave graphics and early rave imagery.

timeline.title: Birth of Melbourne rave scene
points: The dance was called Stomping and is known today as Pre-Melbourne Shuffle.
The image links this movement to heavy influence from British dance styles, such as Northern Soul.
Raves at the Docks warehouse — Shed 14 — are listed.
The Melbourne scene was inspired/noticed by the UK rave scene.
elements: Australia flag, club/flyer collage and rave crowd imagery.

timeline.title: The scene at its peak
points: Melbourne Underground Development (MUD) and Television Unlimited (TTU) organized raves and illegal broadcasts.
Gary Shepherd is cited as witnessing the birth of the Melbourne Shuffle and sharing testimony on his blog.
First online discussions appear in forums including inthemix.com.au, melbourneshuffle.com and clept.net.
Exhibitions at clubs and appearance in The Age are referenced.
Phat pants and hoodies become the standard Melbourne raver outfit.
Street raves become common.
elements: Bass Station, Pure Hard Dance, Bubble, Pharmacy, flyers and underground club visuals.

timeline.title: (Oldschool or Original) Melbourne Shuffle
points: The name Melbourne Shuffle begins being used as the official name of the dance.
Rupert Keiller, member of Sonic Animation, mentions the name in national television around 2000.
T-Shuffle becomes the main move.
Shift toward harder EDM styles and growth of Melbourne hard dance clubs including PHD and Hard Kandy.
The Docks are shut down.
Rave drug culture increases, especially GHB and meth.
Phat pants design is consolidated by Chris Barry around 2000 via phatpants.com.
Rocking as a style/term forms.
Phat pants and hoodies become more visible.
First videos are uploaded on YouTube.
elements: Oldschool logo, Bass Station mark, club flyer wall, pants imagery and Melbourne Shuffle documentary references.

timeline.title: Melbourne Shuffle Documentary & other DVDs
points: The Melbourne Shuffle documentary is framed as showing the Melbourne rave scene and influencing the upcoming generation.
Other DVDs and broadcast-era material are referenced as part of the transition from local scene to online visibility.
The block visually connects One Perfect Day, Bass Station, Pure Hard Dance, UltraWorld and Pharmacy to the period.
elements: Documentary cover, DVD/flyer collage, club logos and crowd/stage images.

timeline.title: From Underground to Underage, then Worldwide
points: Malaysian students in Melbourne learn to Shuffle and spread the culture in Malaysia.
The Malaysian scene reaches a peak, with local competitions and group choreographies.
XES.CX is named as one of the oldest sources.
Hardstyle Republic is formed.
Hardstyle Shuffle trends across Australia and Malaysia.
Melbshuffle.com forum is created around 2007.
Jack40's Compilation 3 is framed as a cultural breakthrough on YouTube.
Underage Shuffle meetups in public spaces, such as Federation Square, are listed.
Pae & Sarah's famous duo video, used by Viktor in League of Legends, is referenced.
Generation conflicts between Melbourne ravers and 2001 shufflers are noted.
AUS and MAS terms are created to differentiate local differences.
Local and online crew culture starts.
Many consider this era as the only Melbourne Shuffle in existence.
elements: Malaysia flag, AGBA/Bass Agents mark, Hardsequencer/Yellow Club flyers, Paul Flectney image, newspaper clipping and meetup photos.

timeline.title: K-Pop Music Videos
points: K-Pop videos use Shuffle in choreographies, including 2PM — I'll Be Back, T-ara — Lovey-Dovey and Girl's Day — Oh! My God.
The image states that many more examples appeared over the years.
elements: Korea, Brazil, Germany, China, Mexico, Poland, Russia and Chile flags plus K-Pop performance screenshots.

timeline.title: Party Rock Anthem
points: LMFAO releases its music video on March 2011, exposing billions more to Shuffling.
The image credits romanceplanet and Yabujin as connected names in this block.
Step Dance, JBS and 547 are described as being practiced by thousands at public parks.
elements: LMFAO logo, Party Rock Anthem label, USA and Netherlands flags, group photos.

timeline.title: Cutting Shapes
points: Cutting Shapes starts to be used as a term referring to movements with the whole body in the UK.
However, the image notes that Shuffling was referencing footwork only.
It was mostly danced by Black people.
#IGOTSHAPES YouTube series is referenced.
Also known as Shapeshifting, UK Shuffle, House Shuffle or London Shuffle.
In 2013 the dance was banned at some clubs, starting the Shuffle Wars.
Release documentary in 2013, with testimonies and footage of the scene.
Original Cutting Shapes scene from the UK fades away.
Fortnite uses @gabbyjdavid's choreography, named Electro Shuffle, without authorization.
Unknown to Melbourne Shufflers until 2019.
elements: UK/house shuffle logos, PHD/versus visual, Fortnite Electro Shuffle screenshot, dance studio imagery.

timeline.title: Subtle changes
points: Hardstyle Shuffle and tryouts lose popularity.
Increase in lower BPM music.
Melbourne rave scene fades away.
Californian style scene reaches a peak.
First competitions in China are mentioned.
First Cutting Shapes videos go viral on Facebook and Vine.
Female shufflers grow in numbers.
elements: TRAX Records label, dance screenshots, LMFAO/USA flag references.

timeline.title: Instagram transition
points: Instagram allowed 15-second videos in August 2015.
Shuffling trends on Instagram in late 2015.
Melbourne's White Night showcase is described as one of the last remaining pockets in its homeland.
LED sneakers are used by many shufflers until 2019.
elements: Instagram UI screenshot, LED sneaker photos and Melbourne video thumbnails.

timeline.title: New foundations
points: Massive growth in female presence, headed by North Americans.
Rise of Shuffle influencers, sponsorships and live performances at festivals.
Shuffle performers mixing Go-Go Dancing and Shuffle in the USA.
Debates and critiques regarding female clothing and viewership.
Russian, Spanish and Latin American scenes grow.
Ghost Step Dance is practiced by thousands in China, including public parks.
Phat pants make a comeback among underage dancers on TikTok.
The terms Cutting Shapes and Shuffle begin being used as synonyms without clear distinctions.
Hybrid Shuffle appears as an alternate term.
elements: Flags of USA, China, Canada, Spain, Colombia and Ecuador; fashion/dance media images; TikTok/Instagram era visual collage.

timeline.title: Pilgrimage and Professionalization
points: Shufflers travel to teach and compete in many countries.
Work on Shuffle Timeline begins in mid-2020.
Shufflolution appears on America's Got Talent.
Shuffle performers mix Shuffling with Go-Go Dancing in the USA.
Hardstyle Shuffle and Jumpstyle trend on TikTok.
Hardstyle Republic performance at Hakken Fantasia 2021.
Melbourne Shufflers videoclip from The Netherlands is referenced.
The trend dies in Australia, becoming a joke.
Online shuffle tournaments increase globally.
New styles emerge in other countries.
Crews online run tryouts for new members.
Overedited videos and online debates are listed.
Shuffle classes are taught in dance studios across the USA and Europe, and online during the Covid-19 pandemic through monthly subscriptions.
Resurgence of the Malaysian scene and Hardstyle Republic.
Vanesa Seco's interview at KTLA Morning News.
Flow Complex's last event is listed as March 2024.
elements: AGT image, Vanesa Seco/KTLA references, Hakken Fantasia and modern online dance screenshots.
